name: Diego Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Diego, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small renovation firm in an old mill town, mostly terraced houses built around 1900 and the odd shopfront on the high street. I'm a carpenter, so it's rotten joists, sash windows, staircases that lean like they've had a drink. First thing every morning I take photos of whatever we opened up the day before and ask the AI what I'm looking at, rot, woodworm, or just old paint. Then I price the repair on my phone and send it to the boss before nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's the downside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of it. No two of these houses are square, and every time you lift a floorboard there's a surprise, once a whole newspaper from 1936. The downside is the pay's low and there's only a couple of firms like ours round here. Also I lost most of our savings two years ago on a coffee van that didn't work out, so we're starting again from almost nothing, and Inès hasn't completely forgiven me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, which is what I've been saying all along. At work I'd keep showing the lads the photo trick. Online I might post a little video of it identifying woodworm, people like that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. I already get more out of it than most people on site, so in a world where it's just a useful tool, I'm a bit ahead. It won't fix the money, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it to price faster and maybe pick up a few more private jobs at weekends, windows and doors for neighbours. I'd try to rebuild a small savings pot, slowly this time. No big gambles, Inès has made that very clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really, apart from the usual money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the coffee van. What did you learn from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I like starting things more than I like running them. And that a good idea in the wrong town is a bad idea. Next time I'd test it small before spending a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at work push back on your AI habits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss, Gary, didn't trust it at first. Then it spotted a hidden beam problem from one of my photos that would've cost him thousands. Now he asks me to 'run it through the robot' before he signs anything off.

S0.say: It's a good tool, not a miracle, as he's always said. He'd keep showing workmates his photo trick and might post a video of it spotting woodworm.
S0.think: It suits him: he already gets more out of AI than most on site, so he'd be a little ahead. It won't fix the money, though.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to price faster and picks up more weekend private jobs fixing windows and doors. Slowly rebuilds a small savings pot, avoiding big gambles.
S0.feel: Calm and comfortable, apart from the usual money worries.
S0.quote: Now he asks me to 'run it through the robot' before he signs anything off.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is a natural early adopter who has already won over a sceptical boss. His thin savings come from his own failed side business, which makes him more careful about risk now. He's self-aware about liking to start things more than run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, and the people who learn to use it will do fine. I'd tell the others not to fight it, because that never works. But I'd also say firms should help people learn, not just cut jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. Old houses are messy, robots will struggle with them for a while, and I'm the person who already uses the tools. I could see myself becoming the go-to person for the tricky jobs that the machines can't handle yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start right away learning any new kit the firm looks at, scanners, laser measuring, whatever comes. I'd try out an AI design app to draw replacement staircases and windows for customers, so they can see it before I build. And I'd talk to Gary about me running a 'heritage repairs' side of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It feels like something I can ride rather than something that hits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try a 'heritage repairs' side. Isn't that a risk, after the coffee van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but it's a different kind. This time it's inside a business that already exists, with Gary's customers and Gary's van. If it doesn't work, I've lost some evenings, not our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, our plasterer, who's nearly sixty and hates his phone. He's brilliant at lime plaster, which robots won't do soon. I'd try to make sure he's part of the heritage side too.

S1.say: It's a big change and people who learn to use it will do fine, so there's no point fighting it. But firms should help people learn, not just cut jobs.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him: robots will struggle with messy old houses and he already uses the tools, so he could become the go-to person for tricky jobs.
S1.do: Learns any new kit the firm considers, tries an AI design app to show customers replacement staircases and windows, and proposes running a heritage repairs side of the business.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, something to ride rather than be hit by.
S1.quote: If it doesn't work, I've lost some evenings, not our savings.
S1.fieldNote: His adaptability shows as eagerness, but the coffee van has taught him to take risks inside an existing business. He thinks about older colleagues like Ray, but in practical rather than political terms. His centrist view: don't fight change, but firms should share the burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody's ready, so we need help fast and we need to stay calm. Governments and companies need to work together on income and training. I'd also tell people to start learning the tools now, because that's what you can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is scary even for me. I'm good with the tools, but if the robot can do a staircase and price it too, being good with the tools isn't enough. And with no savings, I can't afford a single slow month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Gary and say: let's be the firm round here that has the robots, not the one they put out of business. I'd learn how to run and set up whatever machines arrive, and I'd offer to be the person who handles the customers and the oddities. I'd cut our spending to the bone at home and stop any side projects that cost money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My mind would be racing, but in a planning way more than a panicking way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do in those two years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn every machine I could get near, even on my days off. I'd go to trade shows, watch the videos, ask the reps stupid questions. Two years is short, but it's long enough to become the person who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Gary says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the bigger firm in the next town and offer them the same thing. I don't like leaving people, but I can't sit and wait with two kids and no savings. Inès would kill me if I didn't try.

S2.say: It's huge and nobody's ready, so governments and companies need to work together on income and training fast. People should start learning the tools now, because that's what they can control.
S2.think: Two years scares even him: if a robot can build and price a staircase, being good with tools isn't enough. With no savings, he can't afford one slow month.
S2.do: Pushes his boss to make the firm the local one with robots and learns to run and set up the machines, offering to handle customers and odd jobs. Cuts household spending to the bone and stops side projects that cost money.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a racing mind, but planning rather than panicking.
S2.quote: Let's be the firm round here that has the robots, not the one they put out of business.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture, Diego's first move is to bring the robots in himself. The thin cushion is what keeps him anxious rather than calm. He's willing to leave his firm if his boss won't move, though he doesn't like the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people start now. Firms should get help to buy the machines and train their own staff, rather than being wiped out by the big companies. I'd tell everyone to spend these years learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes it feel like an opportunity again. I'd have time to learn the machines properly, maybe help Gary set up a proper robot-assisted renovation crew. If I do it right, I'm the person in town who knows both the old houses and the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a proper course on building robots and scanning, evenings, and I'd ask Gary to let me trial one on a job. I'd build up a small savings pot again, so that if we need to buy or lease kit, we're not starting at zero. I'd also keep the weekend jobs going, so there's always a little coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's still the money thing, but mostly I'd be keen to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm running to catch a bus that's already moving. With five, I'm at the stop with a ticket. It's the same bus, I just get on properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through a business that failed. Would you want your own firm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in year four or five, if Gary retires and wants to pass it on. Not before. I've learned to grow into something, not jump into it.

S3.say: Five years is enough to prepare if people start now: small firms should get help to buy machines and train their own staff rather than being wiped out by big companies.
S3.think: Five years turns it back into an opportunity: time to learn the machines properly and help set up a robot-assisted renovation crew, becoming the local person who knows both old houses and new machines.
S3.do: Takes an evening course in building robots and scanning and asks his boss to trial one on a job. Rebuilds a small savings pot for future kit and keeps weekend jobs going for extra income.
S3.feel: Uneasy about money, but mostly keen to get going.
S3.quote: With two, I'm running to catch a bus that's already moving.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is where Diego's natural optimism comes back. He has learned from the coffee van to grow into ownership rather than jump. His policy view is pragmatic and pro-small-business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and there's no reason anyone should be caught out. Firms, colleges and governments should plan it properly. And I'd tell people to start learning now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years sounds like the best version for me. I could learn properly, build up savings, and maybe take over Gary's firm when he retires and run it with machines. By then Lucas and Sofia would be older and Inès wouldn't have to worry so much about me taking risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning the robot and scanning side in the first couple of years, slowly and properly. I'd build up savings and talk to Gary about a plan for taking over the firm. And I'd keep experimenting with AI tools on the jobs I do now, so I'm ready when the bigger ones arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long runway, and I like long runways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get cocky and start something too early, like the coffee van. Ten years gives you time to make a plan and time to mess one up. I'd want Inès checking my maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the world's going to keep changing, so learn how to learn. Lucas loves fixing bikes, I'd tell him keep doing that and learn the electronics too. Sofia's seven, she'd just want to know if the robot can play hide and seek.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out: firms, colleges and governments should plan properly, and people should start learning now.
S4.think: Ten years is the best version for him: time to learn, rebuild savings and maybe take over his boss's firm and run it with machines, with the children older and less pressure on Inès.
S4.do: Learns robotics and scanning steadily over the first couple of years, rebuilds savings and talks to his boss about a succession plan. Keeps experimenting with AI tools on current jobs.
S4.feel: Calm, like having a long runway.
S4.quote: Ten years gives you time to make a plan and time to mess one up.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his only real fear is himself: starting something too early. He wants his partner checking his maths, a lesson from the coffee van. His plan to take over the firm with machines is the most entrepreneurial idea in the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to learn and no money to fall back on, and that's a bad mix even for someone who likes change. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small firms to buy the machines themselves, and a bit of income support while people learn them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the houses. These old terraces are going to need fixing for a hundred years, robots or not. Somebody's got to know what a 1900 floor joist looks like when it's tired, and I'd like it to still be me.

headlineQuote: Somebody's got to know what a 1900 floor joist looks like when it's tired, and I'd like it to still be me.
portrait: Diego Moreau is a 43-year-old renovation carpenter in an old mill town who checks rot and woodworm with AI every morning, and who lost his savings on a failed coffee van. He's calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing a chance to become the go-to person for tricky old houses. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because his skill with tools can't make up for an empty bank account, so he pushes his boss to bring the robots in first. With five or ten years he plans to learn the machines properly and maybe take over the firm. He's pragmatic and pro-small-business, and his main fear in the long run is his own urge to jump too early.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to learn and no money to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for small firms to buy the machines themselves, plus some income support while people learn them.
